title: Bihar Teen Who Could Not Afford IIT Coaching Wins Diana Award for Mentoring 25,000 Students
excerpt: Adarsh Kumar, now a student at Georgetown University in Qatar, founded the education platform Skillzo at 16 after his own path to coaching in Kota collapsed for want of money. He is one of 49 Indians on this year's Diana Award roll of honour.
body:
• Adarsh Kumar from Bihar has received The Diana Award, the international honour for young people's social action, for founding Skillzo, a platform his university says has connected more than 25,000 students in India with mentorship and career opportunities.
  • Kumar left home to attend IIT-JEE coaching but could not enrol because of financial constraints; he founded Skillzo at 16 after three failed attempts at building organisations.
  • He is among 49 Indians on the 2026 Diana Award roll of honour, which recognised 198 young changemakers from 44 countries.
  • Kumar is also India's first winner of the $100,000 Chegg.org Global Student Prize, and now studies at Georgetown University in Qatar.

Adarsh Kumar grew up in Bihar with the internet as his only guide to a world beyond his textbooks. This month, the founder of the education platform Skillzo has received The Diana Award, the international honour established in 1999 in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, recognising young people for social action and humanitarian work — an award that grew directly out of the opportunities he could not reach himself.

According to Georgetown University in Qatar, where Kumar is a student in the class of 2030, Skillzo has connected more than 25,000 students across India with entrepreneurship education, mentorship and opportunities to explore different careers. He launched the initiative at 16.

"How can I convince, being 16 years old or 17 years old, someone to believe in me?"

— Adarsh Kumar, founder of Skillzo

A detour through Kota

Kumar's own route was the standard one handed to ambitious teenagers in Bihar: leave home, join IIT-JEE coaching, win an engineering seat. Georgetown's account records what happened instead — after three failed attempts at building organisations, financial constraints prevented him from enrolling at the coaching institute he had left home to attend. He describes what felt like rejection becoming redirection: if guidance had been this hard for him to find, other students needed it made accessible.

Convincing adults to take a teenage founder seriously was an early challenge. "Those are the challenges. But you do work, you keep failing, you fail fast," he told the university. His message to other young people is blunt: "Be comfortable with being uncomfortable."

One of 49 Indians honoured

The 2026 Diana Award roll of honour features 198 changemakers from 44 countries, including 49 from India, working on everything from AI-based water testing and low-cost air purifiers to construction safety, eldercare and education. The list was announced on November 4 at the award's virtual ceremony. The award recognises young people aged 16 to 25, selected for leadership, tangible impact, peer empowerment, resilience, integrity and the sustainability of their work.

The Diana Award is not Kumar's first international recognition. He is also the first Indian recipient of the $100,000 Chegg.org Global Student Prize, awarded by Chegg.org and the Varkey Foundation. At Georgetown's Qatar campus he is using the university's five majors to explore academic directions before settling on one, and says he hopes what he learns will contribute to the development of Bihar and India.

What it means

Kumar's story compresses a familiar diaspora arc into a single generation: a student from a small Bihar village, educated partly by the internet, now studying at an American university's Gulf campus while running a platform for the students he left behind. The Diana Award citation suggests the work, not the journey, is the point — 25,000 students mentored is the number the honour rests on.
nri_angle: A Bihar student now at Georgetown's Qatar campus is mentoring students back home at scale — the diaspora's education pipeline running in reverse, from opportunity abroad to guidance for those still trying to reach it.
author: Diaspora Desk
